rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate the elution window for all 10 compounds and identify critical pairs. The midpoint temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

All compounds are well resolved, so halve the gradient duration to reduce the time penalty and measure how the critical pairs respond to slope. Keep the solvent window and temperature unchanged to isolate this effect.

The critical cluster responds strongly to gradient slope. An intermediate duration should recover much of its resolution while keeping the last peak near 9.4 minutes and potentially avoiding the time penalty.

Only one pair remains below baseline resolution. Raising temperature at the same gradient tests whether selectivity can improve that pair while shortening retention and preserving the zero time penalty.

The central peak pattern suggests the critical pair crossed between 40 and 50 °C. A further 5 °C increase may separate it again while retaining sufficient resolution elsewhere and keeping the time penalty at zero.

Slightly steepen the gradient to improve the now-reordered critical pair, which is just below R = 1.5. This modest change should preserve the neighboring pair’s resolution while keeping the time penalty at zero.

Injection 6 has reached the maximum CRF and remains the best method. Test a slightly steeper gradient to shorten elution and modestly improve the limiting pair, while checking that the neighboring pair stays above R = 1.5.
The maximum CRF is already established. Test a higher starting organic fraction with a shallower gradient to seek greater resolution margins around the central cluster while retaining a short run.

Raise the starting fraction another step and make the gradient shallower to seek larger resolution margins than injection 8. The last peak should remain within the gradient and near the zero-time-penalty window, while the first peak should remain retained.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope from injection 9 to recover resolution of the new limiting pair. Its R of 1.41 needs only a modest improvement, and the predicted last-peak time remains below 10 minutes.

With the maximum CRF already secured, test a hotter, shallower gradient for larger resolution margins. The lower starting fraction and gentler slope should help protect the temperature-sensitive neighboring pair while the higher temperature limits retention time.

Return to 55 °C and slightly flatten the slope relative to injection 10 to balance its two closest pairs around R ≈ 1.7. The last peak is expected before 10 minutes, preserving the maximum CRF while potentially improving the resolution margin.
Fine-tune around injection 12 with a slightly steeper slope to balance the two limiting pairs and modestly shorten retention. This should preserve the maximum CRF with a minimum resolution near 1.7.

The maximum CRF is secured, so test a distinct low-temperature selectivity regime for another fully resolved method. The shorter gradient should keep the last peak near the zero-penalty time window despite increased retention at 25 °C.

Test 35 °C against injection 3 to map the cooler side of the critical-pair crossover without changing the gradient. This may improve the pair limiting the 40 °C method while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes; the established CRF 1.000 methods remain the benchmarks.

Test whether a higher starting fraction and shallower slope can resolve the limiting pair at 40 °C without a time penalty. This targets an alternative to the established maximum-score methods at 55 °C.

Raise only the gradient window relative to injection 16, preserving its slope while shortening retention. This tests whether the 40 °C method can retain baseline resolution with more margin below the time-penalty threshold.
Slightly flatten injection 17’s gradient to raise the limiting pair above R = 1.5. The expected last-peak time of about 9.6 minutes should preserve the zero time penalty.

Test a narrower, higher-starting gradient to improve central-pair resolution while offsetting the retention increase from the shallower slope. Injection 18 provides the benchmark; monitor the early pair for compression and the last peak for any time penalty.

Return to the shorter-running 55 °C regime and slightly flatten the slope relative to injection 8. This should preserve maximum CRF while increasing the neighboring pair’s resolution and retaining a comfortable margin below the time-penalty threshold.

Slightly steepen the slope relative to injection 8 to shorten the run while targeting balanced resolution margins for its two closest pairs. Existing maximum-score methods remain secured if the neighboring pair falls below baseline resolution.

Trim the final organic fraction while keeping the slope close to injection 13, which achieved maximum CRF with both critical pairs near R = 1.7. The last peak should elute within the gradient at roughly 9.3 minutes, before the lower final fraction can affect its elution.

Trim injection 8’s gradient endpoint while preserving its starting fraction, slope, and temperature. All peaks are expected to elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, preserving maximum CRF with a shorter programmed gradient.

Trim the endpoint of injection 7, the fastest maximum-score method, while preserving its gradient slope. The last peak is expected near 7.6 minutes, before the gradient ends at the outlet, so resolution and CRF should be retained.

Use the final injection for a local refinement of the maximum-score 55 °C methods, slightly flattening injection 8’s gradient. This should retain baseline resolution for every pair and keep the last peak comfortably below the time-penalty threshold; CRF 1.000 is already secured.
